modules.title: HTTP, HTML, useful JS
modules.subtitle: The bare minimum to understand what AI generates
objectives: Read an HTTP request/response exchange
Recognize minimal semantic HTML
Understand fetch and async in modern JavaScript

contentBlocks.html: In this course you will have AI generate code, then verify it. You cannot verify what you cannot read. This module does not turn you into a front-end developer. It gives you three essential readings (the HTTP dialogue, HTML structure, and async JavaScript) so you understand what AI produces and spot when it gets things wrong.

box.title: Already know all this?
box.body: Phase 0 is optional. If HTTP requests, semantic tags, and async/await are familiar, jump straight to phase 1: nothing on the core path depends on this.

contentBlocks.html: The whole web rests on a simple dialogue. Your browser (the client) sends a request: a method (GET, POST…), a URL, headers (metadata), and sometimes a body. The server sends back a response: a status code, headers, and a body (HTML, JSON, image…). That is it. Every page load, every « Pay » click, every like is a variation of this exchange.

sample.label: Un échange HTTP, à plat
sample.html: // Requête envoyée par le navigateur GET /api/products/42 HTTP/1.1 Host: boutique.example Accept: application/json // Réponse du serveur HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json { "id": 42, "name": "Clavier mécanique", "price": 89 }

contentBlocks.html: Status codes group by family: 2xx = success, 3xx = redirect, 4xx = client-side error (404 not found, 401 not signed in, 403 forbidden), 5xx = server-side error. This reading habit will serve you on every audit: an API that returns 200 with an error message in the body is already a defect to flag.
DevTools habit: open the Network tab (F12), reload a page, and inspect each request: method, status, headers, body. That is your X-ray of the web.

contentBlocks.text: Semantic HTML: structure that means something

contentBlocks.html: HTML describes the nature of content, not its appearance. A title is an <h1>, navigation is a <nav>, an action is a <button>. AI sometimes generates whole pages of clickable <div> elements: it looks like an interface, but it is invisible to keyboard users and screen readers, and search engines penalize it.

sample.label: Le squelette sémantique minimal
sample.html: <header> <nav>…liens principaux…</nav> </header> <main> <h1>Un seul h1 par page</h1> <form> <label for="email">Email</label> <input id="email" type="email" /> <button>Envoyer</button> </form> </main> <footer>…mentions…</footer>

box.title: The classic generated-code trap
box.body: <div onclick=...> instead of <button>, inputs without <label>, five <h1> tags per page. From the Audit phase onward, you will learn to spot and fix these defects systematically.

contentBlocks.html: The modern JavaScript you will see most in generated code comes down to three ideas: fetch to call an API, promises to represent « a result that will arrive later », and async/await to write async code as if it were linear.

sample.label: Appeler une API, la version correcte
sample.html: async function loadProduct() { const response = await fetch("/api/products/42"); if (!response.ok) { // fetch ne rejette PAS sur un 404/500 : à vérifier soi-même throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`); } const product = await response.json(); return product; }

contentBlocks.html: Remember the main trap: fetch only rejects its promise on a network failure. A server that responds with 500 is, from fetch's point of view, a « successful » request. AI-generated code very often forgets the response.ok check. You just learned your first audit check.

contentBlocks.text: Your turn: dissect a network flow

contentBlocks.html: Hands-on exercise (outside the editor): open DevTools (F12) → Network tab on a site you use. Reload the page, pick a request to an API (type fetch/XHR), and note: the method, the URL, the status code, two response headers, and the shape of the body. Then explain in three sentences what this request does for the user. This guided dissection is exactly the move you will repeat in the security audit, phase 8.

quiz.title: HTTP, HTML, JS: check your basics

questions.prompt: What happens when your browser loads a web page?
questions.explanation: The web works in a request → response cycle: the browser asks for a resource, the server answers with a status, headers, and a body (HTML, JSON, image…).

answers.label: It downloads the entire server locally
It sends an HTTP request and receives a response (status + headers + body)
It opens a permanent connection that never closes
It runs the server's code inside the page

questions.prompt: A server responds with « 404 ». What does that mean?
questions.explanation: 4xx = client-side error. 404 specifically: the requested URL matches no resource. A server crash would be 5xx; denied access would be 401/403.

answers.label: The requested resource does not exist

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is conventionally used to create a resource?
questions.explanation: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH/PUT updates, DELETE removes. These conventions let you understand an API without reading its docs line by line.

questions.prompt: Why prefer <button> over a <div onclick>?
questions.explanation: Semantic HTML gives you accessibility for free: keyboard focus, announced role, native behavior. A clickable div must reimplement all of that by hand.

answers.label: The button is keyboard accessible and announced correctly to screen readers
No difference, it is only a style choice

questions.prompt: What does fetch(url) return in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: fetch is async: it returns a promise of Response. You then call response.json() (another promise) to get the data.

answers.label: A promise that resolves to a Response object
The HTML of the current page

modules.title: Git & local project
modules.subtitle: Version cleanly from your first save to Git history
objectives: Use repo, commits, and branches day to day
Keep `.env` separate from versioned code
Run a project's npm scripts

contentBlocks.html: When AI changes ten files at once, only one thing lets you ask « what changed, exactly? » and « go back »: Git. A repo (repository) is the full history of your project. A commit is a named snapshot: the state of the project at a moment in time, with a message that explains why. A branch is a parallel line of work that you combine when it is ready.

sample.label: Le cycle Git de base
sample.html: # créer le dépôt (une fois) git init # voir ce qui a changé : TON outil de contrôle du code généré git status git diff # enregistrer un instantané git add . git commit -m "feat: formulaire de contact avec validation" # travailler sur une branche, puis fusionner git switch -c feature/paiement git switch main git merge feature/paiement

box.title: Golden rule of vibe coding
box.body: One commit before each generation, one commit after each validated iteration. If AI goes off the rails, reviewing the change preview shows the damage and git restore undoes it. Without Git, you are not doing vibe coding, you are playing roulette.

contentBlocks.html: Every real project has secrets: API keys, database passwords, payment tokens. The rule is absolute: a secret never goes in code, and never in Git. It lives in a local .env file that .gitignore excludes from the repo. Why « never »? Because a committed secret stays in history even if you delete the file later, and bots that scan GitHub find an exposed key within minutes.

sample.label: Le trio .env / .env.example / .gitignore
sample.html: # .env : les VRAIES valeurs, jamais commité STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_…vraie clé… DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:motdepasse@host/db # .env.example : la DOC des variables, commité STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=changeme DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@localhost/db # .gitignore : ce que Git doit ignorer node_modules/ .env

box.title: AI hard-codes keys
box.body: Documentation examples that AI learned often contain const apiKey = "sk_live_...". It reproduces that pattern as-is. That is the #1 leak in vibe-coded projects. Phase 8 (Security Audit) dedicates a full module to it, with an automatic scanner.

contentBlocks.html: The package.json file is a JavaScript project's ID card: its dependencies (installed in node_modules/ via npm install; that is why we do not version it, it can be rebuilt) and its scripts. npm run dev is not magic: it runs the command defined under "dev". Always open the package.json of an unknown project: its scripts tell you how to start it, test it, and build it.

sample.label: package.json : la section scripts

contentBlocks.html: Clean project checklist: git init done · .gitignore covers node_modules/ and .env · .env.example documents variables · first commit is readable. That is the goal of the exercise below.

modules.title: Front ↔ API
modules.subtitle: Understand the dialogue between interface and server
objectives: Consume a JSON API from the front end
Handle HTTP errors and basic CORS
Model loading / error / success states

contentBlocks.html: The front end and the server share neither language nor memory: they exchange structured text, almost always JSON. Objects in braces, arrays in brackets, strings, numbers, booleans, null: that is the whole vocabulary. In JavaScript, response.json() turns that text into a usable object, and JSON.stringify() does the reverse to send data.

sample.label: Une réponse d'API typique
sample.html: { "id": 17, "name": "Awa Diop", "email": "awa@example.com", "plan": "pro", "tags": ["beta", "newsletter"], "deletedAt": null }

contentBlocks.text: HTTP errors on the front end

contentBlocks.html: An API call can fail in three different ways, and each is detected differently. 1) The server returns an error (4xx/5xx): fetch still « succeeds », you must test response.ok. 2) The network drops (no connection, DNS, timeout): then the promise rejects, hence try/catch. 3) The body is not the expected JSON: response.json() throws. Robust code covers all three. Rushed generated code often covers none.

sample.label: Les trois familles d'échec
sample.html: try { const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) { // ① le serveur a répondu, mais en erreur (404, 500…) showError(`Erreur ${response.status}`); return; } const data = await response.json(); // ③ peut lever si corps invalide showData(data); } catch (error) { // ② panne réseau, ou JSON invalide (③) showError("Impossible de joindre le serveur."); }

contentBlocks.html: Your front end runs on localhost:5173, the API on another domain. By default, the browser forbids a page from reading a response from another origin (domain + port + protocol): that is the same-origin policy, a fundamental protection. CORS is the mechanism by which the server declares « these origins may call me », via Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Remember the essentials: a CORS error is fixed on the server side (or via a proxy you control), never by hacking the request on the front end.

box.title: CORS is not your enemy
box.body: When AI suggests « disabling CORS » with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on a private API, that is a red flag: it opens your API to the whole world to make an error disappear. The right answer is to list allowed origins explicitly.

contentBlocks.text: Loading / error / success: the contract for every UI

contentBlocks.html: Between the click and the response, time passes. An honest interface shows that time: loading (« working on it »), then success (the data) or error (an actionable message, not a frozen screen). These three states are not cosmetic detail: they are the first criterion on the Design checklist you will apply in phase 9, and the most common omission in generated code, which always assumes everything works on the first try.
Loading: visible as soon as the request starts, never a blank screen.
Error: a clear message + a way to try again.
Success: the data, and an « empty » state planned when the list has nothing.

The exercise below has you implement this full contract against a real public API. It is exactly the skeleton you will find (generated then audited) in every network feature of the product you build from phase 4 onward.

contentBlocks.text: From most guided to most autonomous

contentBlocks.html: « Vibe coding », here, is not « let AI code for you ». It is generate fast, then verify like a professional. Tools range from simplest to most autonomous: a line suggestion while you type, chat for a question, an in-editor assistant (several files), up to agents that read, write, and run commands with little supervision.

box.title: The more the tool acts alone, the more you must verify
box.body: A bad suggestion costs one line. A poorly scoped agent can rewrite your sign-in flow, save a secret to Git history, and propose thousands of lines at once. Hence the Prompt (specify and generate) → Audit (verify with proof) → Ship (deliver with evidence) cycle.

contentBlocks.html: AI is strong at repetitive starter code, common APIs, mechanical rewrites, explanations. It often misses: unwritten business rules, subtle flaws (sign-in, CORS, secrets), unnecessary over-engineering, and code that is plausible but wrong and survives a quick glance.
Habit: if you have not read the change preview, you have not shipped. You hoped.

In production, the model provider does not carry your Stripe incident. You (or your team) sign the integration, the deployment, the promise to the customer. Vibe coding failures without a safety net look alike: blind trust, vague request, skipped review. This course exists to break that pattern.

box.body: Blind trust · unread code · vague request. You will see them again in the autopsy exercise below.

In production, the model provider does not carry your Stripe incident. You (or your team) sign the integration, the deployment, the promise to the customer. Vibe coding failures without a safety net look alike: blind trust, vague request, skipped review. This course exists to break that pattern.

content.title: Traps to name right away
content.body: Blind trust · unread code · vague request. You will see them again in the autopsy exercise below.

questions.prompt: On the AI tools spectrum, what is an agent?
questions.explanation: An agent acts: it can change several files, run commands, iterate. That requires stricter audit than autocomplete.

answers.label: A simple word suggestion in the editor
A system that chains actions (read, write, run) with little supervision

questions.prompt: Which failure is typical of AI-generated code?
questions.explanation: The danger is not unreadable code: it is code that looks correct. Hence systematic audit.

answers.label: It is plausible, passes a quick glance, but hides flaws or nonsense

questions.prompt: Who carries final responsibility for shipped code?
questions.explanation: AI proposes. You ship. In production, your signature is what counts.

answers.label: The developer (or team) who signs and deploys

questions.prompt: Which trap do you avoid by actually reading the generated change preview?
questions.explanation: Accepting without reading means delegating responsibility to a black box. The change preview is your first safety net.

questions.prompt: Why is a vague request (vague prompt) dangerous?
questions.explanation: A vague brief produces vague code. Specifying (Prompt) before generating shrinks the error space.

answers.label: It invents constraints, over-engineers, or drops critical requirements

exercises.title: Autopsy of an AI incident
exercises.instructions: Read the scenario. Check only findings that hold up. Assign consistent severity. Submit your report.
hints: A secret key hard-coded in the repo is almost always critical or high severity.
A TODO comment is not a security flaw on its own.

starterFiles.scenario:
A startup let an AI agent « finish » user sign-in. Two days after go-live, a bot crawls the public mirror repo and finds a Stripe key sk_live_… saved in Git history in src/lib/payments.ts. Fraudulent charges appear. Nobody had read the 1800-line change preview.

Identify root causes and missed signals (not marketing symptoms).

findings.label: Production secret saved in source code
Large batch of changes accepted with no human line-by-line review
No automatic secret scan before integrating code
The React framework is outdated
The README uses too many emojis
Responsibility delegated to the agent (« AI generated it, so it is not on us »)

solutionFiles.__solution: Expected findings: hard-coded secret (critical), unread changes (high), no secret scan before integration (high), denial of responsibility (medium). UI/README distractors are not causes of this incident.

modules.title: The Prompt → Audit → Ship cycle
modules.subtitle: The thread running through the whole course
objectives: Explain why three distinct phases
Describe what you produce at each phase
Prefer small loops over one big tunnel

contentBlocks.html: Mixing specification, generation, verification, and go-live in one rush is the tunnel. We deliberately separate:
Prompt (specify and generate): write the need clearly, then generate a limited proposal.
Audit (verify with proof): check with checklists and evidence (not « looks ok »).
Ship (deliver with evidence): release a version (preview or production) carrying that proof.
Every course phase (sign-in, payments, hosting…) replays this rhythm. You learn not only technical building blocks: you learn a delivery discipline.

A small loop: one micro-feature, a readable change preview, an audit, a partial release. A tunnel: 95 files at once, « we will verify Monday ». The tunnel makes human verification impossible and multiplies forgotten secrets.

box.title: Practical rule
box.body: If you cannot summarize the changes in three sentences, the batch is too big. Split it again before auditing.

contentBlocks.html: The exercise below has you tell healthy steps for a contact form apart from tunnel habits. Later (phases 8 to 12), audit evidence becomes more formal (automatic tools, scores, procedures).

starterFiles.scenario:
Brief: contact page with name, email, message, send to API address POST /api/contact, loading / error / success screen states, no open spam.

A junior asked AI: « build my whole site ». It produced 12 files at once, published an online preview, then « we will audit later ».

contentBlocks.html: For one line: suggestion while you type. For a scoped feature: in-editor assistant with project rules. For multi-file work: an agent, but under a strict brief and with mandatory review. « Assisted review » (AI comments on your changes) helps; it does not replace your judgment on security and business logic.

Project rules tell the assistant which stack you use, which patterns are forbidden, where secrets live. Automatic checks (code quality, secret scanning, dependency review, Lighthouse) produce repeatable evidence. Together they form the Audit phase safety net, even before the business checklists of phases 8 and 9.

contentBlocks.html: Avoid (or watch very closely): home-grown crypto / fine-grained security, critical business logic poorly specified, legal clauses, anything that touches money or personal data directly without a written spec. In those zones, solo vibe coding is a bet, not a method.
